Personality provides a normative framework for characterizing such differences across diagnostic boundaries. Here, we investigated whether personality, particularly agreeableness, relates to behavioral and neural variability in social cognition in autistic young adults without intellectual and language impairment. Thirty-eight autistic participants were compared with a large neurotypical sample for personality and with neurotypical individuals selected with high (HA) or low (LA) agreeableness during three EEG paradigms examining social-interaction perception, basic emotion recognition, and complex mental-state decoding. Autistic participants showed lower agreeableness, extraversion, and conscientiousness and higher neuroticism than neurotypical participants, with substantial interindividual variability. Their agreeableness scores were closer to those of LA than HA participants. Behavioral differences were selective: autistic participants showed lower accuracy than HA participants during complex mental-state decoding, whereas no significant difference was detected relative to LA participants or during the other social-cognitive tasks. Neural activity revealed a more nuanced pattern. No significant group differences emerged during social-interaction perception or basic emotion recognition. In contrast, decoding of complex mental states from the face revealed group differences in the ERP component N170 and a smaller Late Slow Wave (LSW) response in autistic participants. The LSW difference was more extensive relative to HA than to LA neurotypical participants. task has yielded mixed results. A central question is whether negatively cued features can be preemptively suppressed (i.e., before distractors capture attention) or whether they initially capture attention followed by reactive distractor handling (i.e., after distractors capture attention). Notably, negative cueing benefits tend to emerge when the search task is difficult, yet most prior electrophysiological studies have employed easy search tasks that may discourage negative cue use. Therefore, direct neural evidence for negative cueing effects under difficult search is rare. To address this gap, we conducted two experiments. Experiment 1 manipulated task difficulty by varying the number of task-relevant items while keeping the overall set size constant. Results revealed that negative cues enhanced search efficiency in difficult search (8 task-relevant items), but not in easy search (4 items), suggesting that negative cueing benefits depended on the number of items requiring attention rather than overall set size. Experiment 2 employed EEG during difficult search to delineate the neural underpinnings of distractor processing. ERP results showed that negatively cued distractors elicited a reliable early distractor PD in participants showing a cueing benefit in RT but a distractor N2pc on slow-response trials in participants showing RT cost. While preparatory alpha activity did not differ by cue type, stronger alpha lateralization was associated with larger cueing benefits at the individual level. Collectively, these findings suggest that negative cue use is a flexible, strategic and active process, with its deployment contingent on both task demands and individual differences in control Signalling Labs: browser simulations and a read–replicate–explain assessment for teaching neural signalling to psychology students","description":"Neural signalling (the action potential, conduction, synaptic transmission and neurotrans-\nmitter systems) is the most physiological part of an introductory neuroscience course for\npsychology students, and it is often taught from slides alone. This article describes Neu-\nral Signalling Labs, an open learning module of three browser labs with matching student\nbooklets and slide decks. Spike Lab lets students find the threshold, block sodium and\npotassium channels, measure refractoriness and discover rate coding in the Hodgkin–Huxley\nmodel. Relay Lab covers conduction speed and myelin, the steps and summation of chemical\ntransmission, and the actions of agonists, antagonists and reuptake blockers. Prediction Lab\nasks students to replicate Schultz et al. (1997) on dopamine neurons and reward prediction\nerror, and serves as a 90-minute open-book assessment in which students read a classic paper,\nreplicate its main figures and explain them. The labs run on phones and laptops with nothing\nto install and record nothing. They were designed to be neurodivergent-friendly, state every\nsimplification in their models, and are checked by automated end-to-end tests. I describe the\nlearning objectives, instructional design, models, validation and classroom use, and outline a\nplanned evaluation.
